title: Leveraging “Khanmigo” Generative AI-Powered Tool for Personalized Tutoring to Learn Scientific Concepts
extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examined whether using Khanmigo, a generative AI-powered intelligent tutoring system, improved college students’ learning of a science concept relative to other study supports. The paper asks both whether Khanmigo leads to better learning outcomes and how students experience and describe its tutoring behaviors in practice.

The intervention compared three conditions in a short experimental session: a Khanmigo tutoring condition, a Google search condition, and a paper-only condition that emerged post hoc. Participants were 69 undergraduate students in psychology courses at a regional public university in the United States. All students studied lunar phases using the same five-page handout with text and images; the Khanmigo group could ask the AI tutor questions and interact with it, while the search-engine group could use Google, and the paper-only group relied only on the handout. Learning was measured with pre- and post-tests using the Lunar Phases Concept Inventory, and students also completed structured interviews; Khanmigo chat logs were analyzed qualitatively.

Quantitatively, all groups improved from pretest to posttest, but Khanmigo did not produce significantly better gains than Google search or paper-only instruction. Qualitatively, students reported positive experiences with Khanmigo and valued its step-by-step guidance, simplified explanations, practice problems, comprehension checks, and personalized questioning. The authors conclude that Khanmigo may work well as a supplementary scaffold rather than a replacement for traditional instruction, but that brief exposure, limited task demands, and the strength of the paper materials likely reduced the observable advantage of the AI tutor. They recommend longer, more open-ended use cases to better evaluate GenAI tutoring effects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods study with an experimental pretest-posttest comparison and qualitative interviews, but it is not a randomized controlled trial with strong causal control throughout (post-hoc third group, convenience sample, short exposure). The evidence is informative but has notable internal and external validity limitations.
impact_tier_rationale: The study found no measurable achievement advantage for Khanmigo over Google search or paper-only instruction (d=-0.16; no significant treatment effect), so academic impact appears modest/unclear. Qualitative benefits were positive, but they do not establish strong learning impact in this context.

interventions.use_case: Khanmigo use as a generative AI tutor for brief science concept tutoring in lunar phases, where students asked factual and conceptual questions and received step-by-step guidance, prompts, practice problems, and comprehension checks.

finding.finding_summary: Students using Khanmigo did not show significantly greater gains on lunar phases understanding than students using Google search, despite both groups improving from pretest to posttest. On the LPCI difference scores, the Khanmigo vs. Google comparison was not significant (t(67)=-0.649, p>.05, d=-0.16), and the post-hoc 3-group ANOVA also found no significant treatment effect or treatment-by-time interaction.
finding.measure: Lunar Phases Concept Inventory (LPCI) pretest-posttest scores / difference scores
finding.study_size: n=69 (Khanmigo n=22; search-engine n=22; paper-only n=25)

finding.finding_summary: Interview data indicated students perceived Khanmigo positively as engaging, confidence-building, and helpful for asking questions, especially because it offered simple, personalized responses and reduced hesitation to seek help. Students rated its effectiveness around 3.5/5 and described it as useful for support and clarification, though these were short exposure sessions rather than long-term usage.
finding.measure: Structured interview ratings and thematic analysis of student perceptions of engagement, confidence, and helpfulness
finding.study_size: n=22 Khanmigo users in the interview set (within total n=69)

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative findings suggest Khanmigo supported active recall, self-questioning, and comprehension monitoring through prompts, practice problems, and Socratic-style questioning. However, students often bypassed the dialogue and sought direct answers, limiting deeper metacognitive engagement; thus the mechanism was promising but only partially realized in this short session.
finding.measure: Interview themes and analysis of chat logs for questioning, active recall, and comprehension checks
finding.study_size: n=22 Khanmigo users (chat logs and interviews)
